source_basis.authority: National Commission for Indian System of Medicine (NCISM)

scope_note: Complete NCISM-aligned student study layer for Ayushkamiya Adhyaya: verified source Sanskrit verses 1-48, original student meanings, conceptual sections, learning outcomes, examination support and revision structure. Sanskrit source text is preserved as the classical study layer; explanatory meanings are original educational prose.
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and scope of the Ayushkamiya Adhyaya.
Identify the basic concepts of dosha, dhatu and mala and relate them to health and disease.
Explain agni and koshtha at an introductory first-professional level.
Differentiate rasa, guna, virya, vipaka and prabhava as Ayurvedic pharmacodynamic concepts.
Describe the Ayurvedic concepts of health, disease, patient assessment, desha and kala.
Explain the four limbs of treatment and the broad classification of chikitsa.
Apply the basic idea of sadhyasadhyata (prognosis) to clinical reasoning.

sections.title: 1. Ashtanga Hridaya Parichaya
content: Ashtanga Hridaya is a major classical Ayurvedic compendium attributed to Vagbhata. It presents the principal domains of Ayurveda in a comparatively concise and systematic form.
The opening chapter is Ayushkamiya Adhyaya, concerned with the aims of life, preservation of health and the foundations required for rational Ayurvedic practice.

For first-professional study, the chapter should be read as a conceptual foundation: it connects the physician's purpose, the definition of health and disease, assessment of the patient, therapeutic planning and prognosis.

sections.title: 2. Dosha–Dhatu–Mala Parichaya
content: Dosha, dhatu and mala are three foundational functional categories used to understand the state of the body.
Dosha are the principal regulatory factors—Vata, Pitta and Kapha. In a state of equilibrium they support normal physiological activity; disturbance of their normal state is associated with disease.
Dhatu are the seven structural and functional tissue principles: rasa, rakta, mamsa, meda, asthi, majja and shukra. Their normal nourishment and function contribute to bodily integrity.
Mala are waste products whose normal formation and elimination are necessary for physiological balance. The principal bodily malas are purisha, mutra and sveda.
The student should avoid treating these categories as isolated entities. Ayurvedic assessment considers their state, interaction, site, quantity/quality and relation to agni and srotas.

sections.title: 3. Agni and Koshtha
content: Agni denotes the transformative capacity responsible for digestion and metabolism. Its state is central to Ayurvedic assessment because impaired or excessive digestive-metabolic activity can influence nourishment, waste formation and disease processes.
At first-professional level, distinguish the broad concepts of jatharagni, bhutagni and dhatvagni without reducing agni to a single modern physiological process.

Koshtha describes the functional nature of the alimentary tract with respect to bowel tendency and evacuation. It is clinically relevant when considering diet, medicines, procedures and patient response.
Agni and koshtha are assessed together with ahara, bala, prakriti, dosha and disease context rather than as independent labels.

sections.title: 4. Rasa, Guna, Virya, Vipaka and Prabhava
content: Rasa is the primary taste classification used in Ayurveda and is traditionally described through six tastes: madhura, amla, lavana, katu, tikta and kashaya.

Guna refers to qualities used to describe substances and their actions. The twenty commonly taught gurvadi qualities are understood through paired opposites such as guru–laghu, snigdha–ruksha and ushna–shita.
Virya denotes the principal potency through which a substance produces action; ushna and shita are the two broad virya categories commonly taught.
Vipaka refers to the post-digestive effect of a substance, classically discussed through madhura, amla and katu categories.
Prabhava denotes a specific or distinctive action that cannot be adequately explained only from the other known attributes.
These concepts are used together to reason about the expected action of a dravya. They should not be memorised as disconnected definitions.

sections.title: 5. Roga and Arogya
content: Arogya is the state of health; roga denotes a pathological state. Ayurvedic understanding of health is functional and holistic rather than limited to the absence of a named disease.
Health is assessed through the normal state and coordination of dosha, agni, dhatu, mala and related functions, together with mental and experiential well-being.
Disease assessment requires attention to dosha, dushya, srotas, site, cause, stage, strength and the patient's capacity to tolerate and respond to intervention.

sections.title: 6. Roga–Atura Pariksha
content: Roga pariksha concerns examination of the disease, while atura pariksha concerns examination of the patient.
The practical aim is to establish what is affected, why it is affected, how advanced the process is, what the patient's strength is and what therapeutic options are appropriate.
At first-professional level, students should understand examination as a structured reasoning process rather than a list of isolated observations.

sections.title: 7. Desha and Kala
content: Desha refers to place or habitat and may be considered in relation to the patient, disease and medicinal substance. Environmental and geographic context can influence dosha, diet, exposure and treatment response.
Kala refers to time. It includes seasonal and temporal considerations and the stage or duration of a disease process.
Clinical decisions should therefore be contextual: the same presentation may require different consideration depending on place, season, age, stage and other patient factors.

sections.title: 8. Chikitsa Bheda
content: Chikitsa is the planned therapeutic response to a disease with the objective of restoring or supporting normal function and preventing further morbidity.

At introductory level, students should understand the broad distinction between shamana-oriented and shodhana-oriented approaches and recognise that treatment selection depends on dosha, dushya, disease stage, strength, agni, season and suitability.
Therapy is not chosen from the disease name alone. Ayurvedic chikitsa is individualised according to the patient's and disease's characteristics.

sections.title: 9. Pada Chatushtaya
content: The four limbs of treatment are bhishak (physician), dravya (therapeutic substance), upasthata/paricharaka (attendant) and rogi (patient).
The framework emphasises that successful treatment depends on the competence and suitability of all four components, not on the medicine alone.
For examination purposes, learn the four members, their desirable qualities and their interdependence.

sections.title: 10. Vyadhi Sadhyasadhyatva
content: Sadhyasadhyata is the assessment of prognosis and treatability of a disease.

The broad categories taught at introductory level include curable conditions (sadhya) and conditions with increasing therapeutic difficulty or limited curability. Prognosis depends on factors such as disease stage, strength, chronicity, dosha involvement, affected tissues and the presence of complications.
Prognosis is clinically important because it guides the physician in selecting an appropriate therapeutic objective, estimating effort and communicating realistic expectations.

exam_focus: Definitions and introductory significance of Ashtanga Hridaya and Ayushkamiya Adhyaya.
Agni and koshtha: definitions and clinical relevance.
Rasa, guna, virya, vipaka and prabhava: definitions and distinctions.
Roga and arogya; principles of roga and atura pariksha.
Broad chikitsa bheda and the four limbs of treatment.

text_verified_against: Wikisource Sanskrit text of Ashtanga Hridaya Sutrasthana Chapter 1
source_text.note: The Sanskrit layer is provided as the source-text study layer. Student meanings are original explanatory summaries, not a verbatim published translation.

verses.sanskrit: रागादिरोगान् सततानुषक्तानशेषकायप्रसृतानशेषान् । औत्सुक्यमोहारतिदाञ्जघान योऽपूर्ववैद्याय नमोऽस्तु तस्मै ॥१॥
verses.student_meaning: Invocation to the physician who destroys the pervasive afflictions beginning with attachment, delusion and discontent.

verses.sanskrit: आयुः कामयमानेन धर्मार्थसुखसाधनम् । आयुर्वेदोपदेशेषु विधेयः परमादरः॥२॥
verses.student_meaning: A person desiring long life should study and follow Ayurveda with the highest respect because longevity supports the pursuit of dharma, artha and sukha.

verses.sanskrit: ब्रह्मा स्मृत्वाऽऽयुषो वेदं प्रजापतिमजिग्रहत्। सोऽश्विनौ तौ सहस्राक्षं सोऽत्रिपुत्रादिकान्मुनीन् ॥३॥
verses.student_meaning: The traditional transmission of Ayurveda is described from Brahma through Prajapati, the Ashvins, Indra and the sages.

verses.sanskrit: तेऽग्निवेशादिकांस्ते तु पृथक् तन्त्राणि तेनिरे । तेभ्योऽतिविप्रकीर्णेभ्यः प्रायः सारतरोच्चयः ॥४॥
verses.student_meaning: Earlier teachers composed separate treatises; the present work gathers the important essence from widely dispersed teachings.

verses.sanskrit: क्रियतेऽष्टाङ्गहृदयं नातिसंक्षेपविस्तरम् । कायबालग्रहोर्ध्वाङ्गशल्यदंष्ट्राजरावृषान् ॥५॥
verses.student_meaning: Ashtanga Hridaya presents Ayurveda in a balanced concise form and encompasses its eight major branches.

verses.sanskrit: अष्टावङ्गानि तस्याहुश्चिकित्सा येषु संश्रिता । वायुः पित्तं कफश्चेति त्रयो दोषाः समासतः ॥६॥
verses.student_meaning: The eight branches are the fields of Ayurvedic practice; Vata, Pitta and Kapha are the three principal doshas.

verses.sanskrit: विकृताविकृता देहं घ्नन्ति ते वर्तयन्ति च । ते व्यापिनोऽपि हृन्नाभ्योरधोमध्योर्ध्वसंश्रयाः ॥७॥
verses.student_meaning: Doshas in disturbed and undisturbed states respectively damage or support the body; although pervasive, they have characteristic regional predominance.

verses.sanskrit: वयोऽहोरात्रिभुक्तानां तेऽन्तमध्यादिगाः क्रमात् । तैर्भवेद्विषमस्तीक्ष्णो मन्दश्चाग्निः समैः समः ॥८॥
verses.student_meaning: Doshas show sequential predominance across age, day/night and digestion, and their state relates to the four patterns of agni: vishama, tikshna, manda and sama.

verses.sanskrit: कोष्ठः क्रूरो मृदुर्मध्यो मध्यः स्यात्तैः समैरपि । शुक्रार्तवस्थैर्जन्मादौ विषेणेव विषक्रिमेः ॥९॥
verses.student_meaning: Koshtha is described as krura, mridu or madhyama in relation to doshic predominance; constitutional characteristics are also discussed in relation to conception.

verses.sanskrit: तैश्च तिस्रः प्रकृतयो हीनमध्योत्तमाः पृथक् । समधातुः समस्तासु श्रेष्ठा निन्द्या द्विदोषजाः ॥१०॥
verses.student_meaning: Three broad single-dosha constitutional patterns are described, while balanced constitution is regarded as the most favourable and dual-dosha combinations are discussed as less ideal in this classical framework.

verses.sanskrit: तत्र रूक्षो लघुः शीतः खरः सूक्ष्मश्चलोऽनिलः । पित्तं सस्नेहतीक्ष्णोष्णं लघु विस्रं सरं द्रवम् ॥११॥
verses.student_meaning: Vata is characterized by dryness, lightness, coldness, roughness, subtlety and mobility; Pitta by slight unctuousness, sharpness, heat, lightness, spreading and liquidity.

verses.sanskrit: स्निग्धः शीतो गुरुर्मन्दः श्लक्ष्णो मृत्स्नः स्थिरः कफः । संसर्गः सन्निपातश्च तद्द्वित्रिक्षयकोपतः ॥१२॥
verses.student_meaning: Kapha is unctuous, cold, heavy, slow, smooth, slimy and stable; simultaneous involvement of two or three doshas is termed samsarga or sannipata.

verses.sanskrit: रसासृङ्मांसमेदोऽस्थिमज्जशुक्राणि धातवः । सप्त दूष्या मला मूत्रशकृत्स्वेदादयोऽपि च ॥१३॥
verses.student_meaning: The seven dhatus are rasa, rakta, mamsa, medas, asthi, majja and shukra; mutra, shakrit and sveda are principal malas and serve as dushya in disease.

verses.sanskrit: वृद्धिः समानैः सर्वेषां विपरीतैर्विपर्ययः । रसाः स्वाद्वम्ललवणतिक्तोषणकषायकाः ॥१४॥
verses.student_meaning: Like qualities increase corresponding factors and opposite qualities decrease them; six tastes are sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent and astringent.

verses.sanskrit: षड् द्रव्यमाश्रितास्ते च यथापूर्वं बलावहाः । तत्राद्या मारुतं घ्नन्ति त्रयस्तिक्तादयः कफम् ॥१५॥
verses.student_meaning: The six tastes occur in substances and have graded effects; the first three pacify Vata, while bitter, pungent and astringent are grouped as Kapha-pacifying tastes.

verses.sanskrit: कषायतिक्तमधुराः पित्तमन्ये तु कुर्वते । शमनं कोपनं स्वस्थहितं द्रव्यमिति त्रिधा ॥१६॥
verses.student_meaning: Taste combinations influence doshas; substances may be considered as dosha-pacifying, dosha-provoking or beneficial for the healthy.

verses.sanskrit: उष्णशीतगुणोत्कर्षात्तत्र वीर्यं द्विधा स्मृतम् । त्रिधा विपाको द्रव्यस्य स्वाद्वम्लकटुकात्मकः ॥१७॥
verses.student_meaning: Virya is broadly twofold, ushna and shita; vipaka is classically described as madhura, amla or katu.

verses.sanskrit: गुरुमन्दहिमस्निग्धश्लक्ष्णसान्द्रमृदुस्थिराः । गुणाः ससूक्ष्मविशदा विंशतिः सविपर्ययाः ॥१८॥
verses.student_meaning: The twenty gurvadi qualities are taught as ten opposing pairs, providing a framework for understanding the qualities and actions of substances.

verses.sanskrit: कालार्थकर्मणां योगो हीनमिथ्यातिमात्रकः । सम्यग्योगश्च विज्ञेयो रोगारोग्यैककारणम् ॥१९॥
verses.student_meaning: Improper, deficient or excessive interaction with time, sense objects and actions causes disease; proper use supports health.

verses.sanskrit: रोगस्तु दोषवैषम्यं दोषसाम्यमरोगता । निजागन्तुविभागेन तत्र रोगा द्विधा स्मृताः ॥२०॥
verses.student_meaning: Dosha imbalance is disease and dosha equilibrium is health; diseases are broadly divided into nija and agantu according to origin.

verses.sanskrit: तेषां कायमनोभेदादधिष्ठानमपि द्विधा । रजस्तमश्च मनसो द्वौ च दोषावुदाहृतौ ॥२१॥
verses.student_meaning: Disease has two principal loci, body and mind; rajas and tamas are described as the two mental doshas.

verses.sanskrit: दर्शनस्पर्शनप्रश्नैः परीक्षेत च रोगिणम् । रोगं निदानप्राग्रूपलक्षणोपशयाप्तिभिः ॥२२॥
verses.student_meaning: The patient is examined through observation, touch and questioning; disease is examined through nidana, purvarupa, rupa, upashaya and samprapti.

verses.sanskrit: भूमिदेहप्रभेदेन देशमाहुरिह द्विधा । जाङ्गलं वातभूयिष्ठमनूपं तु कफोल्बणम् ॥२३॥
verses.student_meaning: Desha is considered in relation to land and body; jangala is Vata-predominant and anupa is Kapha-predominant.

verses.sanskrit: साधारणं सममलं त्रिधा भूदेशमादिशेत् । क्षणादिर्व्याध्यवस्था च कालो भेषजयोगकृत् ॥२४॥
verses.student_meaning: Bhumi desha is also discussed as jangala, anupa and sadharana; kala includes ordinary time and disease-stage considerations relevant to treatment.

verses.sanskrit: शोधनं शमनं चेति समासादौषधं द्विधा । शरीरजानां दोषाणां क्रमेण परमौषधम् ॥२५॥
verses.student_meaning: Therapeutic measures are broadly divided into shodhana and shamana, with selection determined by the doshic condition and clinical context.

verses.sanskrit: बस्तिर्विरेको वमनं तथा तैलं घृतं मधु । धीधैर्यात्मादिविज्ञानं मनोदोषौषधं परम् ॥२६॥
verses.student_meaning: Classical dosha-specific therapeutic principles are stated, while mental disturbance is addressed through wisdom, steadiness and knowledge of the self and circumstances.

verses.sanskrit: भिषग्द्रव्याण्युपस्थाता रोगी पादचतुष्टयम् । चिकित्सितस्य निर्दिष्टं प्रत्येकं तच्चतुर्गुणम् ॥२७॥
verses.student_meaning: The four limbs of treatment are physician, therapeutic substance, attendant and patient; each has four desirable qualities.

verses.sanskrit: दक्षस्तीर्थात्तशास्त्रार्थो दृष्टकर्मा शुचिर्भिषक् । बहुकल्पं बहुगुणं सम्पन्नं योग्यमौषधम् ॥२८॥
verses.student_meaning: The physician should be skilled, learned, experienced and clean; the medicine should be versatile, well endowed with useful qualities, properly prepared and suitable.

verses.sanskrit: अनुरक्तः शुचिर्दक्षो बुद्धिमान् परिचारकः । आढ्यो रोगी भिषग्वश्यो ज्ञापकः सत्त्ववानपि ॥२९॥
verses.student_meaning: The attendant should be caring, clean, capable and intelligent; the patient should be adequately resourced, cooperative, able to communicate and sufficiently strong.

verses.sanskrit: सर्वौषधक्षमेदेहे यूनः पुंसो जितात्मनः । अमर्मगोऽल्पहेत्वग्ररूपरूपोऽनुपद्रवः ॥३०॥
verses.student_meaning: Favourable prognostic features include adequate tolerance, youth, self-control, absence of vital-site involvement, mild causation and manifestations, and absence of complications.

verses.sanskrit: अतुल्यदृष्यदेशर्तुप्रकृतिः पादसम्पदि । ग्रहेष्वनुगुणेष्वेकदोषमार्गो नवः सुखः ॥३१॥
verses.student_meaning: A readily curable disease is associated with favourable disease factors, compatible patient and environment, complete therapeutic support, single-dosha involvement, single pathway and recent onset.

verses.sanskrit: शस्त्रादिसाधनः कृच्छ्रः सङ्करे च ततो गदः । शेषत्वादायुषो याप्यः पथ्याभ्यासाद्विपर्यये ॥३२॥
verses.student_meaning: Difficult disease may require complex measures; yapya disease is maintained rather than fully eliminated and depends on remaining lifespan and continued wholesome regimen.

verses.sanskrit: अनुपक्रम एव स्यात्स्थितोऽत्यन्तविपर्यये । औत्सुक्यमोहारतिकृद्दृष्टरिष्टोऽक्षनाशनः ॥३३॥
verses.student_meaning: A disease with strongly unfavourable features, severe disturbance, ominous signs and loss of sensory function is classified among conditions not suitable for curative treatment.

verses.sanskrit: त्यजेदातुरं भिषग्भूपैर्द्विष्टं तेषां द्विषं द्विषम् । हीनोपकरणं व्यग्रमविधेयं गतायुषम् ॥३४॥
verses.student_meaning: The text discusses circumstances in which a physician may decline treatment, including lack of necessary resources, inability to cooperate and situations indicating extremely poor prognosis.

verses.sanskrit: चण्डं शोकातुरं भीरुं कृतघ्नं वैद्यमानिनम् । तन्त्रस्यास्य परं चातो वक्ष्यतेऽध्यायसंग्रहः ॥३५॥
verses.student_meaning: Further difficult patient characteristics are listed, followed by a summary of the chapters of the treatise.

verses.sanskrit: आयुष्कामदिनर्त्वीहारोगानुत्पादनद्रवाः । अन्नज्ञानान्नसंरक्षामात्राद्रव्यरसाश्रयाः ॥३६॥
verses.student_meaning: The opening group of Sutrasthana chapters is summarized, beginning with Ayushkamiya, Dinacharya, Ritucharya and Roganutpadaniya.

verses.sanskrit: दोषादिज्ञानतद्भेदतच्चिकित्साद्व्युपक्रमाः । शुद्ध्यादिस्नेहनस्वेदरेकास्थापननावनम् ॥३७॥
verses.student_meaning: The summary continues through chapters on doshas, their types and treatment, purification, oleation, sudation, emesis, purgation, basti and nasya.

verses.sanskrit: धूमगण्डूषदृक्सेकतृप्तियन्त्रकशस्त्रकम् । सिराविधिः शल्यविधिः शस्त्रक्षाराग्निकर्मिकौ ॥३८॥
verses.student_meaning: The Sutrasthana summary continues through chapters on dhumapana, oral and eye procedures, instruments, surgery, venesection, foreign-body removal and cautery.

verses.sanskrit: सूत्रस्थानमिमेऽध्यायास्त्रिंशच्छारीरमुच्यते । गर्भावक्रान्तितद्व्यापदङ्गमर्मविभागिकम् ॥३९॥
verses.student_meaning: The text transitions from the thirty Sutrasthana chapters to Sharira Sthana and identifies its principal subjects.

verses.sanskrit: विकृतिर्दूतजं षष्ठं निदानं सार्वरोगिकम् । ज्वरासृक्श्वासयक्ष्मादिमदाद्यर्शोऽतिसारिणाम् ॥४०॥
verses.student_meaning: The chapter list proceeds to Sharira subjects and then Nidana Sthana, including general and disease-specific diagnostic chapters.

verses.sanskrit: मूत्राघातप्रमेहाणां विद्रध्याद्युदरस्य च । पाण्डुकुष्ठानिलार्तानां वातास्रस्य च षोडश ॥४१॥
verses.student_meaning: The Nidana Sthana summary continues with urinary, metabolic, abdominal, skin, Vata and related disorders.

verses.sanskrit: चिकित्सितं ज्वरे रक्ते कासे श्वासे च यक्ष्मणि । वमौ मदात्ययेऽर्शःसु विषि द्वौ द्वौ च मूत्रिते ॥४२॥
verses.student_meaning: The text then summarizes the major therapeutic chapters dealing with fever, bleeding disorders, cough, dyspnoea, wasting, vomiting, intoxication, piles, diarrhoea and related conditions.

verses.sanskrit: विद्रधौ गुल्मजठरपाण्डुशोफविसर्पिषु । कुष्ठश्वित्रानिलव्याधिवातास्रेषु चिकित्सितम् ॥४३॥
verses.student_meaning: Further Chikitsita chapters address abscess, abdominal masses, abdominal enlargement, pandu, oedema, visarpa, skin disease, Vata disorders and vatashonita.

verses.sanskrit: द्वाविंशतिरिमेऽध्यायाः कल्पसिद्धिरतः परम् । कल्पो वमेर् विरेकस्य तत्सिद्धिर्वस्तिकल्पना ॥४४॥
verses.student_meaning: Kalpa and Siddhi Sthana are summarized, covering emetic and purgative preparations, their complications and basti formulations.

verses.sanskrit: सिद्धिर्वस्त्यापदां षष्ठो द्रव्यकल्पोऽत उत्तरम् । बालोपचारे तद्व्याधौ तद्ग्रहे द्वौ च भूतगे ॥४५॥
verses.student_meaning: The summary includes management of basti complications, pharmaceutics and the beginning of Uttaratantra subjects concerning children and related disorders.

verses.sanskrit: उन्मादेऽथ स्मृतिभ्रंशे द्वौ द्वौ वर्त्मसु सन्धिषु । दृक्तमोलिङ्गनाशेषु त्रयो द्वौ द्वौ च सर्वगे ॥४६॥
verses.student_meaning: Uttaratantra subjects continue through mental disorders and multiple eye-disease diagnostic and therapeutic chapters.

verses.sanskrit: कर्णनासामुखशिरोव्रणे भङ्गे भगन्दरे । ग्रन्थ्यादौ क्षुद्ररोगेषु गुह्यरोगे पृथग्द्वयम् ॥४७॥
verses.student_meaning: The summary continues with ear, nose, mouth, head, wounds, fractures, fistula, tumours, minor diseases and genital disorders.

verses.sanskrit: विषे भुजङ्गे कीटेषु मूषकेषु रसायने । चत्वारिंशोऽनपत्यानामध्यायो बीजपोषणः ॥४८॥
verses.student_meaning: The final summary names poisoning-related chapters and concludes with Rasayana and Vajikarana subjects, completing the overview of the treatise.

concept_map: Eight branches, dosha, agni, koshtha and prakriti (6-10)
Dosha qualities, dhatu, mala and rasa (11-16)
Virya, vipaka, guna and proper/ improper use of time, senses and actions (17-19)
Disease, mind, examination, desha and kala (20-24)
Chikitsa Chatushpada and qualities of physician, medicine, attendant and patient (27-29)
must_memorize: Three doshas and their principal qualities
Two broad viryas and three vipakas
Desha and kala classifications introduced here
Chikitsa Chatushpada and four qualities of each limb
Broad categories of sadhya, yapya and asadhya/prognostic reasoning
Sutrasthana chapter sequence summarized in verses 36-38

long_answer: Explain the eight branches of Ayurveda and their significance.
Describe the three doshas, their qualities and major sites as taught in Ayushkamiya Adhyaya.
Explain the concepts of dhatu, mala, rasa, virya, vipaka and guna.
Explain roga and arogya and describe the examination of the patient and disease.
Describe Chikitsa Chatushpada and the desirable qualities of physician, medicine, attendant and patient.
Explain the principles of sadhyasadhyata and factors influencing prognosis.
short_answer: Enumerate the eight branches of Ayurveda.
Name the three doshas and their principal qualities.
Enumerate seven dhatus and three principal malas.
Name the three methods of patient examination mentioned in the chapter.
Define desha and kala in the context of assessment.
Enumerate the four limbs of treatment.
viva: What is the purpose of studying Ayurveda according to verse 2?
What is the relationship between dosha state and health/disease?
What is the difference between roga pariksha and atura pariksha?
What are the four limbs of treatment?
mcq_topics: Enumeration of dosha, dhatu, mala and rasa

revision_summary: Ayushkamiya establishes the conceptual foundation for studying Ayurveda.
Verses 6-19 build the basic framework of dosha, agni, koshtha, prakriti, dhatu, mala, rasa, guna, virya, vipaka and proper use of time, senses and actions.
Verses 20-26 connect disease, examination, desha, kala and therapeutic principles.
Verses 27-35 establish Chikitsa Chatushpada and prognosis.
Verses 36-48 provide the structural overview of the Ashtanga Hridaya.
